title: The Worst King Turns Around
overview: Manasseh leads Judah into its darkest worship practices, is taken captive, humbles himself and is restored, while his son Amon repeats the wrongs without the change and is killed.

parts.label: Undoing his father's reforms (vv. 1-9)
parts.note: Manasseh rebuilt the hilltop shrines his father Hezekiah had torn down, worshiped other gods and the stars, and put altars and an idol inside the temple meant to carry the LORD's name. He also gave his own children to be burned as offerings and turned to fortune tellers and mediums, and the writer says Judah ended up worse than the nations it had replaced.

parts.label: Taken prisoner (vv. 10-11)
parts.note: After ignoring repeated warnings, Manasseh was captured by Assyrian commanders, bound in bronze chains, and taken to Babylon, a city then under Assyrian rule. The translations differ on one detail: some say he was led with a hook in his nose, while others read the Hebrew differently as taken 'among the thorns' or simply taken captive.

parts.label: A prayer from captivity (vv. 12-13)
parts.note: In prison he humbled himself and prayed, and the LORD listened and brought him back to his throne. The writer presents this as the moment Manasseh finally knew the LORD is God.

parts.label: Rebuilding and cleaning up (vv. 14-17)
parts.note: Back home he strengthened Jerusalem's walls, threw out the idols and foreign altars, and restored the LORD's altar with offerings of thanks. The people kept using the hilltop shrines, now only for the LORD, which still fell short of the law's call to worship at the one temple.

parts.label: Records and burial (vv. 18-20)
parts.note: The writer points to other records of Manasseh's reign and prayer that have since been lost. A later prayer was written in his name, but who wrote it and when is uncertain.

parts.label: Amon's short reign (vv. 21-25)
parts.note: Amon worshiped his father's idols but never turned back, and his own officials killed him after two years. The 'people of the land,' likely Judah's ordinary landholding citizens, executed the plotters and made his young son Josiah king.

disagreement: Christians differ on how this turnaround fits with 2 Kings, which never mentions it and still blames Manasseh for Judah's later fall: some see the two accounts as filling each other out, while others think Chronicles tells the story mainly to show that God answers those who humble themselves.
think: When someone has done serious harm and then truly changes, what do you think it would take for others to believe the change is real?
